\chapter{Verbs at the Core}
\label{ch:pt-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I am, I have, I go, I come, I say, I see and I know in Portuguese, pick the right member of its two be-verbs and its two know-verbs, and name the English words each verb left behind.}

The chapter's last lesson closes the set: after saber and conhecer the reader produces all nine first-person forms in one run - sou, estou, tenho, vou, venho, digo, vejo, sei, conheco - and re-derives the roots behind estar and ter.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ser / estar]{ser / estar — one English verb, two Portuguese ones}

\label{lesson:PT-C18-ser-estar}



\begin{quote}
English has one verb for \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{} Portuguese answers it with two, and this lesson takes them as the single tool they are.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The two-verb kit}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ser — what it is} & \textbf{estar — how it is} \\
\midrule
\textbf{sou, és, é, somos, são} & \textbf{estou, estás, está, estamos, estão} \\
Sou médico. — I am a doctor. & Estou cansado. — I am tired. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One place Portuguese draws the line its own way: marriage. \textbf{Sou casado} — \textquotedblleft{}I am married\textquotedblright{} — uses \emph{ser}, because Portuguese files marital status under what you are. Spanish, the other Iberian daughter of Latin, standardly says \emph{estoy casado} with its \emph{estar} instead. The two languages inherited the same pair of verbs and did not put the same things on each side.

There is even a third verb in the neighbourhood: \textbf{ficar}, \textquotedblleft{}to stay, to end up,\textquotedblright{} which is how Portuguese normally places a town or a building. \textbf{Lisboa fica em Portugal.}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ser} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{esse}}, \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{} English \textbf{is} and \textbf{am} are not borrowings from it; they are inherited relatives, the same ancient word arriving by the Germanic road. From \emph{esse} Latin built \emph{essentia} $\to$ \textbf{essence}, \textbf{essential}; its participle supplies \textbf{present} and \textbf{absent}; and the phrase \emph{inter est}, \textquotedblleft{}it is between, it matters,\textquotedblright{} hardened into \textbf{interest}.

\textbf{estar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{stāre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{stand}, \textbf{state}, \textbf{status}, \textbf{statue}, \textbf{station}, \textbf{stable}, \textbf{estate}, \textbf{circumstance}, \textbf{obstacle}, \textbf{distant}. Every one of them is about standing somewhere, which is exactly what \emph{estar} still reports.

Flag the false friend: \emph{estar} has nothing to do with English \textbf{stare}, which is a Germanic word for gazing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sou, és, é\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}estou, estás, está\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Sou médico; estou cansado.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Sou casado\textquotedblright{} — Portuguese puts this on the \emph{ser} side
  \item the standing family — \textquotedblleft{}estar · state · status · estate\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb names what something is, and which its condition? (\emph{\textbf{Ser}}; \emph{\textbf{estar}}.) Which one does Portuguese use for \textquotedblleft{}I am married\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Ser}} — \emph{sou casado}.) What did \emph{estar}'s Latin source mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{stand}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{stāre}.) Name two English words from it. (\textbf{State}, \textbf{status}, \textbf{estate}, \textbf{circumstance}.) Next: the verb for having.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ter / haver]{ter and há — have, and there is}

\label{lesson:PT-C18-ter-haver}



\begin{quote}
You already know \textbf{ter}, “to have.” Today you will add one small, high-frequency shape from \textbf{haver}: \textbf{há}, “there is” or “there are.”
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Two short patterns}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Tenho pão.} — I have bread. \textbf{Há pão.} — There is bread.
\end{quote}

Use \textbf{ter} when someone has something. Use \textbf{há} when something exists or is present. \textbf{Há} does not change before a plural:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Há um livro.} — There is one book. \textbf{Há dois livros.} — There are two books.
\end{quote}

That is enough for today: \textbf{tenho} points to an owner; \textbf{há} points to what is there.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Haver} comes from Latin \emph{\textbf{habēre}}, “to have.” English \textbf{habit}, \textbf{inhabit} and \textbf{habitat} belong to that family. Portuguese gradually gave most everyday “have” work to \textbf{ter}, but kept \textbf{há} for existence.

English \textbf{have} only looks related to \emph{habēre}: it comes from a different, Germanic family.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “I have bread” — \textbf{Tenho pão.}
  \item “There is bread” — \textbf{Há pão.}
  \item “There are two books” — \textbf{Há dois livros.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb says that someone has something? (\textbf{Ter}.) Which fixed shape says “there is” or “there are”? (\textbf{Há}.) Say “There are two books.” (\textbf{Há dois livros.}) Next, you will reuse \textbf{há} for one new meaning.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[há três anos]{há três anos — three years ago}

\label{lesson:PT-C18-ha-time-ago}



\begin{quote}
You know \textbf{há} as “there is.” Add one nearby meaning: before a length of time, \textbf{há} can mean “ago.”
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: One reusable frame}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{há três anos} — three years ago \textbf{há dois dias} — two days ago
\end{quote}

Build it as \textbf{há + amount of time}. Keep \textbf{há} fixed; the number and time word tell you how far back to look.

Say the frame slowly: \textbf{há … três … anos}. Then say it as one small unit: \textbf{há três anos}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} “two days ago” — \textbf{há dois dias}
  \item \emph{Say it:} “three years ago” — \textbf{há três anos}
  \item \emph{Choose:} Does \textbf{há} change? (\textbf{No.})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What comes after \textbf{há} in this pattern? (\textbf{An amount of time.}) Say “three years ago.” (\textbf{Há três anos.}) You have added one meaning without mixing it into the earlier existence lesson.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ter que]{ter que — to have to}

\label{lesson:PT-C18-ter-que}



\begin{quote}
You know \textbf{tenho}, “I have.” Add \textbf{que} and a verb to express one obligation.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: One reusable frame}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Tenho que falar.} — I have to speak.
\end{quote}

Build it in three pieces:

1. \textbf{tenho} — I have 2. \textbf{que} — the link 3. \textbf{falar} — to speak

Only \textbf{ter} changes with the person. The following action stays in its dictionary form: \textbf{temos que falar}, “we have to speak.”

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} “I have to speak” — \textbf{Tenho que falar.}
  \item \emph{Say it:} “We have to speak” — \textbf{Temos que falar.}
  \item \emph{Choose:} Does \textbf{falar} change here? (\textbf{No.})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Complete the frame: \textbf{tenho … falar}. (\textbf{Que.}) Say “We have to speak.” (\textbf{Temos que falar.}) One new construction, practised in one small step.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ir]{ir — two letters, three ancestors}

\label{lesson:PT-C18-ir}



\begin{quote}
Portuguese's verb for \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} is two letters long, and no two of its rows resemble one another. There is a reason for that.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The forms, and the future they build}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{vou} & nós \textbf{vamos} \\
tu \textbf{vais} & vocês/eles \textbf{vão} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{vai} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Its preterite is \textbf{fui, foste, foi, fomos, foram} — the row Chapter 16 showed \emph{ir} borrowing wholesale from \emph{ser}.

The everyday future runs through this verb: \textbf{ir} plus an infinitive.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Vou falar com ele.} — \textquotedblleft{}I am going to speak with him.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

English builds its own casual future the very same way, out of its own verb for going. And \textbf{vamos} on its own is \textquotedblleft{}let's go.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
The infinitive \textbf{ir} comes from Latin \emph{\textbf{īre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to go.\textquotedblright{} The \emph{vou} row comes from a different verb, \emph{\textbf{vādere}}, \textquotedblleft{}to advance.\textquotedblright{} The preterite comes from a third source entirely, the old perfect of \emph{esse}.

From \emph{īre} English holds a large family, all built by prefix: \textbf{exit} (\emph{ex- itum}, \textquotedblleft{}gone out\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{transit} (\textquotedblleft{}gone across\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{initial} (\emph{in-itium}, \textquotedblleft{}a going in,\textquotedblright{} so a beginning), \textbf{itinerary}, \textbf{ambition} (\emph{amb-īre}, \textquotedblleft{}to go around\textquotedblright{} canvassing for votes), \textbf{perish} (\emph{per-īre}, \textquotedblleft{}to go all the way through\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{obituary} (\emph{ob-īre}, \textquotedblleft{}to go to meet\textquotedblright{} death). Even the grammar word \textbf{preterite}, the tense of Chapter 15, is \emph{praeter-itum}, \textquotedblleft{}gone past.\textquotedblright{}

From \emph{vādere}: \textbf{evade}, \textbf{invade}, \textbf{pervade} — and English \textbf{wade}, which is not a borrowing at all but a Germanic cousin of the same ancient root.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vou, vais, vai, vamos, vão\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Vou falar com ele\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Vamos!\textquotedblright{}
  \item the going family — \textquotedblleft{}exit · transit · initial · ambition\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{ir}. (\textbf{Vou, vais, vai, vamos, vão}.) How do you say \textquotedblleft{}I am going to speak\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Vou falar}}.) Which verb lends \emph{ir} its preterite? (\emph{\textbf{Ser}} — \emph{fui, foste, foi}.) Which Latin verb gives the infinitive? (\emph{\textbf{Īre}}.) Name two English words from it. (\textbf{Exit}, \textbf{transit}, \textbf{initial}, \textbf{ambition}, \textbf{perish}.) Next: coming.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vir]{vir — coming, and the n that dissolved}

\label{lesson:PT-C18-vir}



\begin{quote}
The opposite of \emph{ir} is \textbf{vir}, and it is short for exactly the reason \emph{mão} is short.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The forms, and two traps}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{venho} & nós \textbf{vimos} \\
tu \textbf{vens} & vocês/eles \textbf{vêm} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{vem} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two things to watch:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{vem} (\textquotedblleft{}he comes\textquotedblright{}) against \textbf{vêm} (\textquotedblleft{}they come\textquotedblright{}). The circumflex marks the plural and the sound barely moves — the same trick \emph{tem} and \emph{têm} play in Chapter 14. Portuguese lets an accent carry grammar.
  \item \textbf{venho} has the \emph{-nh-}, Portuguese's palatal \emph{ny}, met already in \emph{vinho} and \emph{tenho}.
\end{itemize}

Useful on day one: \textbf{Vem cá.} — \textquotedblleft{}Come here.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vir} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{venīre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to come.\textquotedblright{} Take out the \emph{-n-} between vowels and \emph{venīre} collapses to \emph{vir} — the same regular Portuguese change that turned \emph{manus} into \textbf{mão} and \emph{lūna} into \textbf{lua}. The \emph{-nh-} forms are where the nasal survived instead of vanishing.

English kept the whole verb, prefix by prefix. A \textbf{venue} is \textquotedblleft{}a coming\textquotedblright{}; an \textbf{advent} and an \textbf{adventure} are things coming \emph{toward} you (\emph{ad-}); to \textbf{convene} is to come together (\emph{con-}), which gives \textbf{convenient} and \textbf{convention}; to \textbf{intervene} is to come between; to \textbf{prevent} was to come \emph{before} (\emph{prae-}); to \textbf{invent} is to come upon something. \textbf{Revenue} is what comes back, an \textbf{avenue} is the way a thing comes in, an \textbf{event} is what comes out (\emph{ex-}), and a \textbf{souvenir} is a memory coming up from below (\emph{sub-}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}venho, vens, vem, vimos, vêm\textquotedblright{}
  \item the accent pair — \textquotedblleft{}ele \textbf{vem} · eles \textbf{vêm}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Vem cá\textquotedblright{}
  \item the coming family — \textquotedblleft{}venue · advent · convene · invent\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{vir}. (\textbf{Venho, vens, vem, vimos, vêm}.) What separates \emph{vem} from \emph{vêm}? (The \textbf{circumflex} — singular against plural.) Why is the infinitive only three letters? (The \emph{\textbf{-n-}} \textbf{dissolved between vowels}, as in \emph{mão}.) Name two English words from \emph{venīre}. (\textbf{Venue}, \textbf{advent}, \textbf{convene}, \textbf{prevent}, \textbf{event}.) Next: saying.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dizer]{dizer — saying, and the verb that judges}

\label{lesson:PT-C18-dizer}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Falar} is to speak, in general. \textbf{Dizer} is to say a particular thing — and it hands you the most useful question a beginner owns.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The forms, and the question}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{digo} & nós \textbf{dizemos} \\
tu \textbf{dizes} & vocês/eles \textbf{dizem} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{diz} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The first person breaks ranks: \textbf{digo}, with a hard \emph{g}, where every other form keeps a buzzing \emph{z}. That swap is old and regular, and it recurs across this family of verbs.

Now the question. Chapter 2 gave you \emph{como}, \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Como se diz…?} — \textquotedblleft{}How does one say…?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

That one line will get you through a conversation you are not ready for. The past participle is \textbf{dito}, \textquotedblleft{}said\textquotedblright{}, as in \emph{dito e feito} — \textquotedblleft{}said and done.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dizer} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{dīcere}}, \textquotedblleft{}to say, to point out.\textquotedblright{} Its participle stem \emph{dict-} is scattered through English: \textbf{dictate}, \textbf{dictation}, \textbf{dictionary}, \textbf{diction}, \textbf{dictator}; \textbf{verdict}, which is \emph{vērum dictum}, \textquotedblleft{}a true saying\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{predict} (\textquotedblleft{}say beforehand\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{contradict} (\textquotedblleft{}say against\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{edict}, \textbf{benediction} (\textquotedblleft{}a good saying\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{addict}, from \emph{ad-dictus}, \textquotedblleft{}spoken over to\textquotedblright{} someone.

The older sense, \textquotedblleft{}to point,\textquotedblright{} survives in \textbf{indicate} and \textbf{index} — \emph{in-dicāre} is to point \emph{at} a thing.

And the prize: a Roman \emph{iūdex} was the man who \emph{speaks the law} — \emph{iūs}, \textquotedblleft{}law,\textquotedblright{} welded to \emph{dīcere}. English took him as \textbf{judge}, and the family as \textbf{judicial}, \textbf{judgement}, and \textbf{prejudice}, a saying made in advance.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}digo, dizes, diz, dizemos, dizem\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Como se diz…?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dito e feito\textquotedblright{}
  \item the saying family — \textquotedblleft{}dictate · verdict · edict · judge\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{dizer}. (\textbf{Digo, dizes, diz, dizemos, dizem}.) Which form breaks the pattern? (\emph{\textbf{Digo}}, with a hard \emph{g}.) How do you ask how something is said? (\emph{\textbf{Como se diz…?}}) What is a \emph{verdict}, taken apart? (\emph{Vērum dictum} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a true saying}\textquotedblright{}.) Where does \textbf{judge} come from? (\emph{Iūs} plus \emph{dīcere} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he who speaks the law}\textquotedblright{}.) Next: seeing.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ver]{ver — seeing, and a form that means two things}

\label{lesson:PT-C18-ver}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ver}, \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} is short for the same reason \emph{vir} is: a consonant wore away in the middle. It also produces Portuguese's most confusable single form.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The forms, and the collision}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{vejo} & nós \textbf{vemos} \\
tu \textbf{vês} & vocês/eles \textbf{veem} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{vê} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Vejo} takes a \emph{j} that no other form has. Its completed past is \textbf{vi, viste, viu, vimos, viram}, and the participle is \textbf{visto}, \textquotedblleft{}seen\textquotedblright{} — the same word as the noun \textbf{vista}, \textquotedblleft{}a view,\textquotedblright{} which English borrowed whole.

Now the collision. \textbf{Vimos} is \textquotedblleft{}we saw\textquotedblright{} here, and \textquotedblleft{}we come\textquotedblright{} for \emph{vir}. Nothing in the form tells them apart; the sentence around it does.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Vimos o mar.} — \textquotedblleft{}We saw the sea.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Vimos de Lisboa.} — \textquotedblleft{}We come from Lisbon.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ver} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{vidēre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to see.\textquotedblright{} The \emph{-d-} between vowels wore away, as it did in dozens of Portuguese verbs, leaving three letters.

English owns the rest of the verb: \textbf{vision}, \textbf{visible}, \textbf{visit}, and \textbf{video}, which is simply Latin for \textquotedblleft{}I see.\textquotedblright{} With prefixes: \textbf{evident} (\emph{ex-}, \textquotedblleft{}seen out in the open\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{provide} and \textbf{providence} (\emph{prō-}, \textquotedblleft{}to see ahead\textquotedblright{}) — and \textbf{prudent}, which is nothing but \emph{providens} worn down. Also \textbf{survey} and \textbf{supervise} (\emph{super-}, \textquotedblleft{}to see over\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{review}, \textbf{interview}, and \textbf{advice} with \textbf{advise}, from \emph{ad vīsum}, \textquotedblleft{}according to what has been seen.\textquotedblright{} Even \textbf{envy} is here: \emph{in-vidēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to look upon\textquotedblright{} someone with ill will.

One false friend. English \textbf{very} is \emph{not} from this verb; it comes from \emph{vērus}, \textquotedblleft{}true\textquotedblright{} — the same \emph{vērum} sitting inside \textbf{verdict}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vejo, vês, vê, vemos, veem\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vi, viste, viu, vimos, viram\textquotedblright{}
  \item the collision — \textquotedblleft{}Vimos o mar · Vimos de Lisboa\textquotedblright{}
  \item the seeing family — \textquotedblleft{}vision · evident · provide · survey\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{ver}. (\textbf{Vejo, vês, vê, vemos, veem}.) What two things can \emph{vimos} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{We saw}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{we come}\textquotedblright{}.) What happened to \emph{vidēre}'s \textbf{-d-}? (It \textbf{wore away between vowels}.) Which English word is \emph{providens} worn down? (\textbf{Prudent}.) Is \emph{very} part of this family? (\textbf{No} — that is \emph{vērus}, \textquotedblleft{}true\textquotedblright{}.) Next: knowing, in two flavours.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[saber / conhecer]{saber / conhecer — two ways to know}

\label{lesson:PT-C18-saber-conhecer}



\begin{quote}
This chapter opened with one English verb answered by two Portuguese ones. It closes with the second such pair — and this one hides a flavour.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Which knowing is which}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{saber — facts and skills} & \textbf{conhecer — people and places} \\
\midrule
\textbf{sei, sabes, sabe, sabemos, sabem} & \textbf{conheço, conheces, conhece, conhecem} \\
Sei a resposta. — I know the answer. & Conheço o Pedro. — I know Pedro. \\
Sei nadar. — I know how to swim. & Conheço Lisboa. — I know Lisbon. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Saber} is knowing \emph{that} something is so, or knowing \emph{how} to do a thing. \textbf{Conhecer} is being acquainted with a person, a city, a book. French splits the idea the same way, with \emph{savoir} and \emph{connaître}; English merged the two and lost the distinction entirely.

\textbf{Sei} is worth its own breath: it is irregular, it is short, and \textbf{não sei}, \textquotedblleft{}I don't know,\textquotedblright{} is the sentence you will need first.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{saber} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{sapere}}, which meant \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to taste}\textquotedblright{} long before it meant \textquotedblleft{}to have good taste, to be wise.\textquotedblright{} Portuguese kept both jobs in the one verb: \textbf{sabe bem} means \textquotedblleft{}it tastes good,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{sabor} is \textquotedblleft{}flavour.\textquotedblright{} English split the halves between two borrowings — the taste half as \textbf{savour} and \textbf{savoury}, the wisdom half as \textbf{sapient}, the word inside \emph{Homo sapiens}, and \textbf{sage}. Something \textbf{insipid} is \emph{in-sapidus}, \textquotedblleft{}without taste.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{conhecer} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{cognōscere}}, which is \emph{co-} (\textquotedblleft{}thoroughly\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{gnōscere} (\textquotedblleft{}to get to know\textquotedblright{}). English holds the compound as \textbf{cognition}, \textbf{recognise}, \textbf{incognito}, \textbf{notice}, \textbf{notion}, and, through French, \textbf{connoisseur} — the very same verb. That second piece is also the root English \textbf{know} itself grew from, so \emph{conhecer} and \emph{know} are distant relatives after all.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sei, sabes, sabe\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}conheço, conheces, conhece\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Não sei\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Conheço Lisboa\textquotedblright{}
  \item the whole chapter, first person — \textquotedblleft{}sou, estou, tenho, vou, venho, digo, vejo, sei, conheço\textquotedblright{}
  \item the taste still inside the verb — \textquotedblleft{}sabe bem\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb knows a fact, and which knows a person? (\emph{\textbf{Saber}}; \emph{\textbf{conhecer}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I don't know.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Não sei}}.) What did \emph{sapere} mean first? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{To taste}\textquotedblright{} — still live in \emph{sabe bem}.) Now the nine of this chapter, in the \emph{eu} form. (\textbf{Sou, estou, tenho, vou, venho, digo, vejo, sei, conheço}.) And their roots: which one came from \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Estar}}, from \emph{stāre}.) Which from \textquotedblleft{}to hold\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Ter}}, from \emph{tenēre}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
